nameStory: The black-billed cuckoo gets its straightforward name from its distinctive dark bill, which helps distinguish it from its yellow-billed cousin. The word 'cuckoo' itself comes from the bird's call, mimicking the sound they make - though our New England species sounds quite different from the famous 'cuckoo clock' call of European cuckoos.
description: The black-billed cuckoo is a slender, secretive bird about the size of a robin but much more elongated. It has a sleek brown back, white underparts, and a notably long tail with white spots underneath. These mysterious birds are more often heard than seen, slipping quietly through dense foliage with their curved bills and striking red eye-rings. They're summer visitors to New England, arriving in late spring to breed in our woodlands.

idTips.label: Bill Color
idTips.description: Look for the all-black bill that gives this bird its name - it's completely dark without any yellow coloring, feeling smooth and slightly curved if you ever handle a banded bird

idTips.label: Red Eye-Ring
idTips.description: A bright red ring around the eye creates a striking contrast against the bird's subdued brown and white plumage - this fiery circle is often the first feature that catches your attention

idTips.label: Tail Pattern
idTips.description: The long tail shows small white spots on the underside tips of the feathers, visible when the bird flies or spreads its tail - these spots are much smaller than those of its yellow-billed relative

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notice the sleek, elongated silhouette with a slim neck and long tail that makes up about half the bird's total length - they move with a fluid, almost snake-like grace through branches

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Listen for a distinctive 'cu-cu-cu-cu' call that sounds like a series of wooden knocks, often described as more hollow and rhythmic than musical

habitat: Black-billed cuckoos prefer dense woodlands and forest edges with thick understory growth, especially areas with young trees and shrubs. You'll find them in deciduous and mixed forests, overgrown fields reverting to woodland, and riparian areas with dense vegetation. They favor spots with plenty of caterpillars, particularly during outbreaks of tent caterpillars and gypsy moths.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in New England in mid to late May, when their distinctive calls become most frequent as they establish territories and seek mates. This is the best time to hear them calling.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for observing black-billed cuckoos as they nest and raise young through July and August. Look for them moving quietly through dense foliage hunting caterpillars.
seasonality.fall: Becomes increasingly quiet and secretive as they prepare for migration, typically departing by early September. Much harder to detect during this period.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, spending the winter in South America. Any cuckoo-like bird seen in winter would be a very rare vagrant.

funFact: Unlike their European relatives that famously lay eggs in other birds' nests, black-billed cuckoos usually raise their own chicks - though they'll occasionally 'cheat' and sneak an egg into another bird's nest when they're running behind schedule!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the yellow-billed cuckoo, but remember 'black bill, small spots' versus 'yellow bill, big spots' - the black-billed has smaller white tail spots and lacks any yellow on the bill. The red eye-ring is also more prominent on the black-billed cuckoo.
contextualKnowledge: Many people expect cuckoos to sound like cuckoo clocks, but that's based on European cuckoos - our American cuckoos have completely different calls and are much more secretive birds. They're also sometimes called 'rain crows' because of the old belief that their calls predict rain.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative, the yellow-billed cuckoo, the black-billed has an all-dark bill (versus yellow with black on top), smaller white tail spots, and a more prominent red eye-ring. Black-billed cuckoos also prefer denser forest habitats while yellow-billed cuckoos like more open woodlands and edges. The black-billed's call is typically more of a rapid 'cu-cu-cu' series, while yellow-billed gives slower, more spaced notes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo is larger and more colorful than its Black-billed Cuckoo relative, with that bright yellow lower bill, prominent white tail spots, and rusty wing patches that the Black-billed lacks.
